operationalization: Simulate second-order rule 37R on finite rings from many initial conditions and track a disorder measure, the recurrence time, and the fraction of the state space visited. The claim is confirmed if disorder fluctuates without a systematic rise and orbits stay non-ergodic and non-trivially long; it is refuted if disorder rises monotonically to equilibrium or the evolution is the short-period repetitive type.

candidate_datasets.name: Golly
candidate_datasets.role: open cellular-automaton simulator in which rule 37R can be rerun on closed finite lattices

candidate_datasets.name: A New Kind of Science online
candidate_datasets.role: public specification of rule 37R and the closed-system evolutions to recompute

obstacles: Any finite reversible system eventually recurs, so 'indefinitely' has to be read relative to the recurrence time.
A cellular-automaton disorder measure is only a proxy for thermodynamic entropy.
rationale: The rule, the closed finite setting, and the alternatives (monotonic randomization, or simple repetition as in rules 0R and 90R) are fully specified, and Wolfram already records a concrete period for one run. Re-simulation with a fixed disorder statistic can confirm or refute the non-monotonic, non-ergodic behavior at practical sizes. The thermodynamic-limit reading of the Second Law is the main residual interpretation, not a missing dataset.

operationalization: Compare measures of spatial order inside living systems with the presence and lifetime of membrane-bounded compartments, holding energy throughput fixed. The claim would be supported if compartmentalization accounted for more of the maintained order than open-system free-energy flux; it would be weakened if order tracked metabolism across uncompartmentalized or membrane-disrupted systems.

candidate_datasets.name: Cell Image Library
candidate_datasets.role: public cell images showing membrane-bounded compartments, not a causal test of order

candidate_datasets.name: BioNumbers
candidate_datasets.role: compiled quantitative cell-biology values, including compartment and membrane scales

obstacles: Compartmentalization is confounded with metabolism and free-energy throughput.
'The main mechanism' has no agreed partition of credit across biological systems.
rationale: Public cell images and quantitative compilations establish that organisms are partitioned by membranes and that local order exists while cells persist. They do not separate that partitioning from energy flux, export of entropy, or self-organization in open systems, which are the serious rivals. The causal 'mainly' claim is therefore only partly approachable with existing data.

operationalization: Survey entropy-production time series for closed and isolated natural systems and test for a uniform trend toward randomness versus long-lived non-monotonic fluctuations. A large class of systems with no systematic trend would support the claim; a restriction of failures to brief microscopic fluctuations would support only a much weaker exception.

candidate_datasets.name: NIST Chemistry WebBook
candidate_datasets.role: public thermodynamic properties of macroscopic substances, which cover equilibrium Second-Law behavior rather than fluctuation histories

obstacles: Microscopic fluctuation theorems already qualify the Second Law without systems behaving like rule 37R.
No public census samples natural systems widely enough to support or refute 'many'.
rationale: Equilibrium thermodynamic tables and scattered small-system experiments can test pieces of the claim: macroscopic matter usually thermalizes, and short-time entropy decreases occur. They do not constitute a representative sample of natural systems evolving without a trend toward randomness. The universal-sounding qualification of the Second Law is only partly constrained.

operationalization: Average the density of particle-conserving block cellular automata over initial conditions with a fixed coarse density profile and fit the result to the diffusion equation. Agreement in the stated randomizing, conserving case confirms the exhibited mechanism; a conserving randomizing rule whose coarse density does not diffuse, or a fluid whose continuum limit needs extra structure, limits the 'whenever'.

candidate_datasets.name: Golly
candidate_datasets.role: open simulator for rerunning block cellular automata and averaging density

candidate_datasets.name: SageMath
candidate_datasets.role: open system for fitting averaged density profiles to the diffusion equation

obstacles: The universal quantifier covers fluids and every discrete conserving system, not only the illustrated block rules.
Long-lived correlations, which Wolfram notes in one of his own examples, can block an exact diffusion limit.
rationale: The block-automaton demonstration is fully specified and can be rerun: averaged density either approaches the diffusion equation or it does not. Hydrodynamic limits are proved for some related lattice systems, so the mechanism is not merely visual similarity. The word 'whenever', extended to fluids and arbitrary discrete rules, is wider than those checks.

operationalization: There is no decision criterion that separates 'the only realistic method' from rival search strategies, because the target ultimate rule is not an identified object with a recorded discovery path.
obstacles: Failure of inverse engineering does not show that it cannot work, and a successful search would not show it was the only practical method.
The target rule is unknown, so there is no outcome that counts as finding it.
rationale: The claim is a judgment about methodology: working backwards from known laws will not realistically yield a simple ultimate rule, and blind search is the only practical route. No public dataset records attempts against a known target, and either success or failure of a strategy can be redescribed to fit the claim. It has no measurable consequence that would settle it.

operationalization: Fix a class of candidate universe rules, enumerate a large sample, and score which of continuous space, gravitational and quantum features, particle-mass ratios, and spatial dimension appear. The claim is supported if the first group recurs across many rules while mass ratios and dimension stay rule-specific; it is refuted if those 'generic' features are as rare as the mass spectrum.

candidate_datasets.name: Wolfram Physics Project
candidate_datasets.role: public sample of evolving candidate rules, too small to estimate which features are generic

obstacles: There is no agreed enumerable class of candidate rules for the universe.
A survey large enough to separate generic from rule-specific features is far beyond a weeks-scale computation.
rationale: The contrast between generic and rule-specific features is meaningful once a rule class is fixed, and it would be settled by enumeration rather than by new laboratory measurements. Published rule explorations are a small, self-selected sample and do not score gravitation, quantum features, and mass spectra side by side. The necessary computational survey does not exist.

operationalization: Classify published physical laws by whether they are derived as large-scale limits of a more microscopic theory or are inputs with no such derivation, then ask whether the simple derived laws constrain the microscopic rule. A census in which most textbook laws are effective theories supports the claim; a finding that most laws are irreducible inputs would refute the 'vast majority'.

candidate_datasets.name: Particle Data Group
candidate_datasets.role: catalog of particle-physics parameters, separating measured inputs from quantities fixed by an effective theory

candidate_datasets.name: NIST Chemistry WebBook
candidate_datasets.role: macroscopic thermodynamic and fluid properties that standard derivations treat as emergent

obstacles: 'Truly fundamental' is defined only relative to an unknown ultimate rule.
There is no canonical list of 'physical laws discovered so far' on which to compute a majority.
rationale: Many familiar laws, including continuum thermodynamics and fluid mechanics, already have published derivations from more microscopic models, so that part of the claim can be checked. Particle data show other regularities still put in by hand. Without a census of laws and without the ultimate rule, 'the vast majority' and the claim that their simplicity says little about that rule stay only partly tested.

operationalization: Compare scattering and other short-distance probes with a continuum cross-section down to a stated length, and look for a breakdown that a discrete substrate would produce below about 10^-20 m. Continuum behavior at all accessible scales leaves the discreteness claim untouched; a scale-dependent deviation fitted by a discrete cutoff would support it.

candidate_datasets.name: Particle Data Group
candidate_datasets.role: compiled experimental limits on short-distance physics and tests of pointlike continuum behavior

candidate_datasets.name: CERN Open Data
candidate_datasets.role: public collider datasets underlying current lower bounds on any discreteness scale

obstacles: Present null results are what the claim predicts, since it places discreteness below the probed scale.
No public dataset reaches the distances at which discrete elements are asserted to exist.
rationale: Collider compilations can reconfirm that space behaves as a continuum down to roughly the scale Wolfram names. That reconfirmation does not discriminate discreteness at still smaller distances from a continuum at all scales. The positive claim needs shorter-distance data that have not been collected.

operationalization: No observable is specified that would differ between a universe in which space and matter are the same structure and one in which matter is additional data on a spatial substrate, once both reproduce current physics.
obstacles: 'Simplest' and 'same stuff' are ontological preferences, not measured variables.
A cellular-automaton-like split between space and contents can be made empirically equivalent by pushing the split below current resolution.
rationale: The claim is that the simplest ultimate model should build matter from the same structure as space. Simplicity here is a modeling preference, and every current observation is compatible both with that identification and with matter as separate content on a background. Nothing public distinguishes the two.

operationalization: Derive a signature that is produced by a trivalent network substrate and not by other discrete spaces, then compare it with short-distance or cosmological measurements. A unique matched signature would support the claim; a theorem that every rival substrate produces the same signature would leave it unresolved.

candidate_datasets.name: Wolfram Physics Project
candidate_datasets.role: public trivalent-network models and large-scale limits, not a measurement of physical space

candidate_datasets.name: Particle Data Group
candidate_datasets.role: experimental constraints on spacetime at accessible scales, with no network-valued variables

obstacles: Causal sets, spin networks, and lattices can match the same large-scale three-dimensional observations.
Trivalence is stated as sufficient, so a different node degree would not by itself refute the network claim.
rationale: A network with only connectivity, including the trivalent case, is a definite hypothesis and could in principle be distinguished by a small-scale signature. Existing particle and cosmological constraints, and published network evolutions, do not isolate that signature from other discrete substrates. The data that would decide it are absent.

operationalization: For a graph, compute the number of nodes within graph distance r and test whether it grows as r^d; compare with lattices, trees, and random graphs, and with the theorem that ball volume in R^d grows as r^d. Polynomial growth of that degree supports a finite dimension d; exponential or irregular growth refutes a finite ordinary dimension.

candidate_datasets.name: MathWorld
candidate_datasets.role: public statement of ball-volume growth in d-dimensional Euclidean space

candidate_datasets.name: SageMath
candidate_datasets.role: open graph computation of node counts within distance r for lattices, trees, and random graphs

obstacles: Growth like r^d is necessary for a manifold limit; without local regularity it is not sufficient for ordinary space.
Oscillating or position-dependent growth has to be handled by the limiting sense the claim already allows.
rationale: The growth test is explicit, and the continuum fact Wolfram invokes is the standard volume of a d-dimensional ball. Lattices, trees, and random graphs are immediate confirming and refuting examples and can be counted directly. The remaining caveat is local Euclidean structure, which the claim's 'limiting sense' already flags rather than leaving the test undefined.

operationalization: Build the causal network of a mobile automaton and test whether the update order is recoverable from that network alone, and whether a sequential update can be sliced as synchronized parallel steps. Recovery of the microscopic schedule from the network would refute the claim for that system; success only shows the result for embedded toy observers.

candidate_datasets.name: A New Kind of Science online
candidate_datasets.role: public mobile-automaton examples whose causal networks are fully specified

candidate_datasets.name: SageMath
candidate_datasets.role: open recomputation of updating events and causal networks

obstacles: For an observer defined to see only causal relations, the result holds largely by construction.
The extension from mobile automata to human perception of time is not in the computable examples.
rationale: The toy systems are fully specified, and it is a finite check whether their causal networks omit the update schedule while still presenting parallel slices. That settles the computational illustration. It does not test the further claim about observers in the universe, because nothing in the simulation corresponds to a measured perception of time.

operationalization: Prove that replacement rules whose blocks cannot overlap themselves or each other never interfere, and check that every application order builds the same causal network; compare with an overlapping block that yields two networks. Identity of the networks confirms the claim; a non-overlapping rule with two causal networks refutes it.

candidate_datasets.name: A New Kind of Science online
candidate_datasets.role: public non-overlapping and overlapping substitution examples used as the theorem's instances

candidate_datasets.name: SageMath
candidate_datasets.role: open enumeration of application orders and comparison of the resulting causal networks

obstacles: Wolfram's weaker proviso, that overlaps need only be absent on strings the system actually generates, must be checked separately from purely syntactic non-overlap.
rationale: Non-overlap is a syntactic condition, and the causal network is a finite combinatorial object of the rewrite history. Non-interfering rewrites are order-independent by a short confluence argument, and overlapping blocks supply counter-models. Both the proof and an exhaustive check of small rule sets are within standard methods.

operationalization: Once a candidate rule for the universe is fixed, test whether every allowed update order produces one causal network. A rule that reproduces observed physics and is causally invariant would support the claim; a rule that reproduces physics only along some orders, with observable branching, would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Wolfram Physics Project
candidate_datasets.role: public candidate rewrite rules and causal networks, not an identification of the universe's rule

obstacles: A unique perceived history is also predicted by ordinary continuum spacetime, so it does not isolate causal invariance.
The actual update rule is unknown, so the property cannot be evaluated on the object the claim is about.
rationale: Causal invariance is a sharp property of a rewrite system, and it is checkable for any fully specified rule. The claim applies it to the universe's actual rules, which are not in hand, and the single history we observe does not distinguish that mechanism from standard relativistic spacetime. Settling it requires either those rules or a new signature of non-invariance.

operationalization: Measure spatial dimension from large-scale physics, and separately evolve network rules with and without small-scale randomness, estimating dimension from node growth. Robust dimension 3 only in the random ensemble would support the mechanism; dimension 3 arising equally from ordered networks, or random networks failing to lock dimension 3, would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Particle Data Group
candidate_datasets.role: experimental physics formulated in three-dimensional space, with no test of a network mechanism

candidate_datasets.name: Wolfram Physics Project
candidate_datasets.role: public network evolutions on which graph dimension can be estimated for a small sample of rules

obstacles: Many models set dimension to 3 directly, so the observed dimension does not show that randomness is the cause.
Estimating a stable dimension on large random networks is a specialist computation, not a weeks-scale survey.
rationale: That physical space has three dimensions is already the working content of existing particle and cosmological data, so that fragment of the claim is settled. The further claim that small-scale network randomness is what makes dimension 3 robust is a mechanism, and published network samples are too few to separate it from rules that impose dimension directly.

operationalization: Compute the Planck length and Planck time from measured c, G, and hbar and compare them with the stated 10^-35 m and 10^-43 s, and check that their ratio equals c. Agreement of the ratio and of the order of magnitude is required by the definitions; a measured elementary length far from the Planck length would refute the numerical guess.

candidate_datasets.name: CODATA recommended values via NIST
candidate_datasets.role: public values of c, G, and hbar from which Planck length and Planck time are computed

obstacles: Once every causal edge is assigned one elementary length and one elementary time, their ratio is a fixed speed by definition and is identified with c rather than measured.
No experiment measures an elementary length near 10^-35 m; current data only leave that scale allowed.
rationale: The numerical guesses are the Planck scales, which follow at once from public constants, and the ratio of those defined scales is c. That checks the arithmetic and the identification Wolfram states. It does not test whether causal-network edges have those lengths, because no dataset contains a discreteness scale.

operationalization: For a causally invariant network, compare the rules induced on spacelike slices at different angles and derive the time-dilation factor as a function of velocity. Quantitative agreement with the relativistic factor on those models supports the derivation; angle-dependent rules, or a dilation factor other than 1/sqrt(1-v^2/c^2), refute it for that class.

candidate_datasets.name: Particle Data Group
candidate_datasets.role: experimental status of special-relativistic effects such as time dilation in particle data

candidate_datasets.name: CODATA recommended values via NIST
candidate_datasets.role: measured value of c used in the relativistic time-dilation formula

obstacles: Experiments confirm special relativity without distinguishing a causal-network mechanism from Minkowski spacetime.
The slice argument is explicit for regular networks; it is not a finished theorem for arbitrary causally invariant rules.
rationale: Time dilation and the independence of physics from uniform velocity are established experimentally, and the geometric clock argument can be checked on the regular causal networks Wolfram draws. Those checks do not show that causal invariance is why relativity holds, because the same phenomena follow from continuum special relativity. A general derivation for irregular networks remains incomplete.

operationalization: Identify persistent localized structures in a network model of space and match their conserved attributes and interaction rules to the elementary-particle spectrum. A one-to-one match with no particle-specific rules would support the claim; a spectrum that cannot be realized by persistent network structures would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Particle Data Group
candidate_datasets.role: measured particle types, charges, and masses that a network structure would have to reproduce

candidate_datasets.name: Golly
candidate_datasets.role: open examples of localized structures in class 4 cellular automata, an analogy rather than a particle measurement

obstacles: Solitons, strings, and other localized-structure models fit the same particle data.
Resemblance to class 4 gliders does not test whether physical particles are network tangles.
rationale: Particle properties are catalogued in detail, and localized structures in class 4 rules are easy to simulate. Neither resource connects a persistent network tangle to an electron or a quark. The claim stays a hypothesis until a model produces the spectrum, and no such public dataset exists.

operationalization: Test published lepton and quark masses for simple rational or other pre-registered relations, then repeat the test on a stated definition of mass with interaction energy removed. Simple relations among observed masses would confirm the strong reading; their absence only touches the claim if the interaction-energy subtraction is fixed in advance.

candidate_datasets.name: Particle Data Group
candidate_datasets.role: high-precision measured masses of leptons and quarks

obstacles: 'May' plus an allowance for interaction energy makes the claim hard to refute.
How much of a measured mass is interaction energy depends on the renormalization scheme.
rationale: Observed masses are public and precise, and it is immediate that they do not lie in simple ratios. The claim retreats to unknown fundamental masses after subtracting a scheme-dependent interaction energy, so the tables test only the surface reading. The hedged remainder is not fixed tightly enough for those tables to confirm or refute it.

operationalization: Expand the number of nodes at graph distance r, which Wolfram takes to grow as r^(d-1) in flat space, and compare the first correction with the Riemannian expansion of geodesic-sphere area in the scalar curvature. A leading correction proportional to the Ricci scalar times r^(d+1), and to no other curvature invariant, confirms the claim; a different exponent or a leading tensor invariant refutes it.

candidate_datasets.name: MathWorld: Scalar Curvature
candidate_datasets.role: public reference for the Ricci scalar in the standard geometric expansion

candidate_datasets.name: SageMath
candidate_datasets.role: open checks of node counts against curvature on example triangulated surfaces

obstacles: The expansion assumes a smooth Riemannian limit at large r; a raw network matches it only after that limit.
Wolfram's count is the shell at distance r, whose correction scales as r^(d+1); the ball volume correction scales differently.
rationale: Wolfram counts nodes reached at distance r, a shell growing as r^(d-1), and states that the first correction is the Ricci scalar times r^(d+1). That is the standard area expansion of geodesic spheres, which is a published theorem, not a fit to a picture. Example networks with positive and negative curvature can be counted as a numerical check of the same expansion.

operationalization: For network rewrite rules that are causally invariant and hold dimension fixed, test whether the large-scale curvature satisfies the vacuum Einstein condition that the Ricci tensor vanishes, against rules that conserve dimension but produce other curvature equations. A general proof or a quantified survey would confirm 'almost inevitably'; a positive-measure family of counterexample rules would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Wolfram Physics Project
candidate_datasets.role: public special-case arguments from causal invariance toward the Einstein equations

candidate_datasets.name: Gravitational Wave Open Science Center
candidate_datasets.role: public tests of general relativity, which do not identify the underlying network rules

obstacles: 'Almost inevitably' quantifies over an undefined class of rules.
Vacuum Einstein behavior can emerge from more than one continuum limit, so a matching equation does not isolate the stated hypotheses.
rationale: The vacuum Einstein condition and the causal-invariance and fixed-dimension hypotheses are mathematically meaningful, and special-case arguments plus the lattice-gas analogy to Navier–Stokes exist. They do not amount to a theorem that almost every such rule yields the Einstein equations. Gravitational-wave tests constrain the macroscopic equation, not the claim about network rules.

operationalization: List a fixed set of quantum-theory features, such as amplitudes, interference, measurement outcomes, and identical-particle statistics, and test whether a causally invariant network model reproduces them without putting in the quantum formalism. Reproduction of the pre-registered list would support the claim; failure on a core feature after the model is fixed would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Particle Data Group
candidate_datasets.role: experimental quantum phenomena a network model would have to recover

candidate_datasets.name: Wolfram Physics Project
candidate_datasets.role: public network programs offered as candidate models, without a completed match to quantum theory

obstacles: 'Many if not all key features' does not name the checklist, so partial successes can always be counted as enough.
Building realistic models of quantum experiments inside these programs is a large unfinished computation.
rationale: Quantum phenomena are abundantly measured, and network programs are public, but the claim is that those programs will reproduce quantum theory. No existing dataset or finished derivation shows that they do, and the phrase 'key features' is loose enough that scattered resemblances would not decide it. A pre-registered match remains to be produced.

operationalization: Compare measured correlations of entangled pairs with the quantum predictions, and separately exhibit a deterministic network whose extra-spatial threads reproduce those correlations, including the strength of the violation. A working thread model confirms the possibility claim; measured correlations are already known and do not by themselves test the mechanism.

candidate_datasets.name: NIST
candidate_datasets.role: public record of loophole-free Bell tests measuring the correlations at issue

candidate_datasets.name: Particle Data Group
candidate_datasets.role: review of particle properties and quantum foundations relevant to entanglement experiments

obstacles: Standard quantum mechanics and other deterministic hidden-variable pictures with extra connections fit the same correlations.
An existence claim ('can arise') is confirmed only by an explicit model and is barely refuted by unsuccessful attempts.
rationale: Bell-type correlations are measured and publicly documented, so the phenomenon the mechanism is meant to explain is not in doubt. The thread explanation is an existence claim about deterministic networks, and no public model is tight enough that the measured correlations confirm or refute it rather than quantum theory in general. Only the empirical half is currently testable.

operationalization: Take standard tasks in perception and in statistical or mathematical analysis and test whether a short rule-based program matches human or textbook performance on public stimuli. Success on a task supports the claim for that task; a basic perceptual or analytic capacity that remains unmatched by any simple program would limit the universal reading.

candidate_datasets.name: Laboratory for Computational Vision texture collection
candidate_datasets.role: public textures used to test simple filter models of visual perception

candidate_datasets.name: CRCNS
candidate_datasets.role: public neuroscience recordings against which simple perception programs can be compared

obstacles: 'Basic mechanisms' and 'simple rules' have no agreed size cutoff.
Matching a task with a short program does not show that the human mechanism is that program.
rationale: Many perceptual and analytic tasks already have simple algorithmic models, and public texture and neural datasets can test particular ones. The claim covers human perception and scientific analysis in general. Existing resources speak to examples, not to the assertion that the basic mechanisms as a class are captured by simple rules.

operationalization: Generate output from a declared class of simple programs, give standard inference methods only the output, and measure how often they recover the rule within a resource bound. Frequent recovery would refute 'extremely difficult'; recovery only for traditionally simple rules, and failure on complex-output rules, would support the contrast.

candidate_datasets.name: Golly
candidate_datasets.role: open generation of cellular-automaton output whose rules can be withheld from an inference procedure

candidate_datasets.name: OEIS
candidate_datasets.role: public sequences, including cellular-automaton columns, against which inferred rules can be checked

obstacles: 'Extremely difficult' needs a cost threshold.
There is no algorithm that inverts arbitrary programs, so the result depends on the size cutoff of the search.
rationale: For elementary cellular automata the outputs are trivial to generate and the rule space is finite, so inversion difficulty can be measured now for that class. Traditional low-complexity rules are the natural control, and they are often easy to guess. The claim's scope is 'general simple programs', which is larger than any one finished survey.

operationalization: Treat Kolmogorov complexity as the definition that calls a string random only when it has no short description, and use the known proof that this complexity is uncomputable and infinite for no computable sequence. That confirms the restrictiveness and uncomputability clauses; it does not decide whether every useful definition must mention the search for descriptions.

candidate_datasets.name: MathWorld: Kolmogorov Complexity
candidate_datasets.role: public statement of description-length complexity and its uncomputability

obstacles: The conclusion about what is useful is a normative judgment about definitions.
Uncomputability of complexity is compatible with pragmatic randomness tests that never claim to find every short description.
rationale: The premises are theorems: description-length randomness is uncomputable, and every sequence from a deterministic rule has a short description, so that definition never counts those sequences as random. Those premises can be checked from the published theory now. The further claim that any useful definition must refer to the method of finding descriptions is not a mathematical or empirical proposition.

operationalization: The sentence proposes how the word 'random' should be used. Applying the proposed test to data illustrates the definition; it does not confirm or refute the recommendation to adopt it.
obstacles: A stipulative definition is not settled by the data it classifies.
'Essentially no simple program' is not itself a decidable property, so the definition does not yield a finite test.
rationale: Wolfram is offering a definition: call something random when essentially no simple program detects regularities in it. That proposal can be adopted or rejected on grounds of usefulness, which is the subject of the surrounding argument, but no dataset confirms or refutes a stipulation. The empirical companion claim, about how rarely further programs succeed, is separate.

operationalization: Take sequences and images that pass a fixed set of standard tests, then enumerate simple programs up to a length cutoff and measure how often another program detects a regularity. A high rate of extra detections would refute 'extremely rare'; a near-zero rate inside the cutoff supports the claim only inside that cutoff.

candidate_datasets.name: NIST Random Bit Generation
candidate_datasets.role: public statistical test suites corresponding to standard regularity checks

candidate_datasets.name: OEIS
candidate_datasets.role: public sequences that can be screened by standard tests and by further short programs

obstacles: The space of simple programs is unbounded, so 'any other simple program' can be searched only up to a size limit.
A regularity can be invisible to every test in a chosen finite set without being absent.
rationale: Standard test suites and large sequence archives exist, and enumerating very short programs is feasible. That can estimate how often a further short program finds structure after a few standard tests fail, for a bounded class. It cannot cover every simple program, so the claim's unrestricted rarity statement stays only partly tested.

operationalization: The claim equates calling something complex with a failure to find a short description of chosen features. Changing which features are chosen changes the verdict by the claim's own terms, so there is no independent measurement that would refute it.
obstacles: Complexity is defined relative to the observer's chosen features, so the claim cannot fail against an observer-independent dataset.
The sentence is an account of what the word means, not a prediction about particular objects.
rationale: Wolfram defines apparent complexity as the failure of our perception and analysis to find a short description of the features we care about. That is a conceptual identification, and the dependence on chosen features is part of the definition rather than a parameter to estimate. No public measurement would confirm or refute it.

operationalization: Classify images by whether human observers have a short description of some features but not others, then measure looking time and preference against purely random and purely simple controls. Preference peaking on the mixed class would support the claim; equal or higher preference for random or purely simple images would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: OpenNeuro
candidate_datasets.role: public neuroimaging repository in which visual-preference studies, if present, are a scattered subset

obstacles: Aesthetic preference and attention are task-dependent, and 'aesthetically pleasing' has several competing scales.
No single public dataset uses Wolfram's partition into simply describable versus indescribable features.
rationale: Intermediate-complexity preference is a known empirical question, and looking time is a measurable variable. Existing public materials do not line up with the specific contrast among random images, simply patterned images, and images whose features split into describable and indescribable. The claim is testable in part through related studies and is not settled by one open dataset.

operationalization: Run run-length, Huffman or block, pointer-based, and two-dimensional compressors on uniform, repetitive, nested, and complex cellular-automaton patterns, including patterns from very short programs. Similar strong compression only for the first three classes confirms the claim; substantial compression of a complex short-program pattern by a generic method refutes it.

candidate_datasets.name: GNU gzip
candidate_datasets.role: public general-purpose compressor representing pointer-based and dictionary methods

candidate_datasets.name: Golly
candidate_datasets.role: open generator of repetitive, nested, and complex cellular-automaton patterns

obstacles: A compressor designed around one particular automaton can compress that automaton; the claim is about generic methods aimed at repetition and nesting.
'No substantial compression' depends on length and on a numerical threshold.
rationale: The pattern classes and the compressor families are concrete, and both the generators and standard compressors are public. Compression ratios can be compared in days. The result decides the claim for the generic methods Wolfram names; it does not forbid a purpose-built encoder for one chosen rule.

operationalization: Compress simple, random, and complex images with a JPEG-style transform at a range of rates, optionally permuting the retained coefficients, and score whether the relevant features remain recognizable. Survival of simple and random images at rates where complex images become unrecognizable would support the claim; equal recognition thresholds would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: JPEG
candidate_datasets.role: official specification of the transform coding scheme the claim generalizes

candidate_datasets.name: Independent JPEG Group
candidate_datasets.role: public JPEG implementation for recomputing lossy compressions

candidate_datasets.name: Golly
candidate_datasets.role: open source of simple, nested, and complex images to compress

obstacles: 'Recognizable' is a human judgment; an error metric is only a proxy.
Quantization tables and the choice of basis change which features survive.
rationale: The compression procedure itself is standard and the source images can be regenerated, so the computational half can be rerun now. Whether features remain recognizable is a perceptual variable, and public data do not already contain judgments on this exact image partition. Reordering coefficients can be tested computationally; the recognition criterion still needs an observer or an agreed proxy.

operationalization: Represent textures by densities of a fixed set of local templates and test whether those densities predict human discrimination as well as joint statistics or less structured image measures. Prediction from densities, with cortical responses matching the templates, would support the claim; systematic failures on textures that share densities but differ in dependencies would refute the density account.

candidate_datasets.name: Laboratory for Computational Vision texture collection
candidate_datasets.role: public textures and parametric models used to test local-feature accounts of texture discrimination

candidate_datasets.name: Allen Brain Map
candidate_datasets.role: public cortical cell data relevant to whether visual cells act as fixed local templates

obstacles: Some texture pairs are discriminated by joint statistics even when marginal feature densities match.
The broader claim that perception in general ignores everything but fixed features exceeds texture data.
rationale: Texture discrimination by local-feature statistics is a standard, operational hypothesis, and public texture sets plus cortical atlases contain the relevant variables. Those data support a density or summary-statistic account for many textures and also contain known counterexamples that need higher-order structure. The claim's extension to perception in general, by analogy with color, is wider than this test.

operationalization: Show observers two-dimensional patterns that are purely periodic or nested, excluding cases dominated by large uniform regions, and compare detection accuracy with a pointer-based encoder that flags the nesting. High accuracy for repetition and chance accuracy for nesting would support the claim; reliable visual detection of nesting would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: CRCNS
candidate_datasets.role: public visual-neuroscience and psychophysics recordings; nested-versus-repetitive pattern tests are only sparsely represented

obstacles: Symmetry and repetition detection are well studied; nesting as Wolfram defines it is not a standard stimulus class in public archives.
A new forced-choice experiment would be new data collection, which is outside existing resources.
rationale: The contrast is experimentally sharp: periodic patterns versus nested patterns, with a simple encoder as the existence proof that the nesting is objectively present. Published work on symmetry detection covers the easy half. Public datasets do not contain a systematic human test of nested cellular-automaton patterns, so that half of the claim is only sparsely constrained.

operationalization: Synthesize sounds from sequences that are periodic, nested, or otherwise non-repetitive but spectrally matched, and test whether listeners identify structure beyond pitch and a few spectral peaks. Identification limited to repetition at definite frequencies would support the claim; reliable detection of nested or other non-repetitive structure would refute 'essentially nothing else'.

candidate_datasets.name: CRCNS
candidate_datasets.role: public auditory-neuroscience datasets; listening tests on nested discrete-sequence sounds are not a standard holding

obstacles: Listeners also report timbre, envelope, and speech-like structure, so the stimulus class 'fairly uniform sequences' has to be enforced.
Sounds that carry nested structure are scarce in existing listening-test archives.
rationale: Pitch and the hearing of periodic sounds are heavily measured, which covers the positive half of the claim. The negative half, that nested or other non-repetitive structure is heard as noise, needs stimuli built from discrete sequences of the kind Wolfram considers. Those comparisons exist mainly as scattered studies, not as a dataset matched to the claim's scope.

operationalization: Fit block-frequency, Markov, and probabilistic cellular-automaton models to data from deterministic cellular automata, matching the statistics used in the fit, then compare typical model samples with the original on features not in the fit. Samples that match the fitted statistics but are more random and miss the detailed features confirm the claim; samples that reproduce those features refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Golly
candidate_datasets.role: open generator of deterministic cellular-automaton data to which probabilistic models can be fitted

candidate_datasets.name: SageMath
candidate_datasets.role: open fitting of Markov and block-frequency models and comparison of typical samples

obstacles: A probabilistic model with enough hidden state can be made to copy the data, so the model class has to stay the ones named.
'More random' needs a pre-registered feature score beyond the fitted statistics.
rationale: The model classes and the data source are fully specified, and both fitting and resampling are standard. Agreement on the fitted statistics together with a loss of detailed structure is a direct confirming pattern; reproduction of those details is a direct refutation. The check is a computation on generated data, not a new experiment.

operationalization: Take an explicit sequence such as a linear-feedback shift-register output or the concatenation of the binary representations of the integers, compute block frequencies, and apply a second regularity test such as the spread of those frequencies or the linear recurrence. Accurate block frequencies together with a detected regularity refute the claim that equal block frequencies are a universal randomness test.

candidate_datasets.name: OEIS Champernowne constant
candidate_datasets.role: public digits of a concatenated-integer constant with strong frequency properties and a simple construction

candidate_datasets.name: OEIS
candidate_datasets.role: public shift-register and other simply generated binary sequences used as counterexamples

obstacles: Equality of frequencies for every block length is an infinite condition; a proof uses the construction rather than a finite table of counts.
rationale: The claim is the negation of a proposed universal test, and it is settled by counterexample. Shift-register sequences and digit concatenations are public, simply generated, and known to have balanced block frequencies while remaining non-random by an independent check. One verified counterexample refutes universality; no broader dataset is required.

operationalization: Apply block-frequency tests and a declared set of simple cellular automata to the center column of rule 30 and to a long prefix of the binary expansion of pi. A statistically significant deviation on either sequence refutes the claim for that analysis; passage of both analyses supports the claim as a statement about detectable deviation, not as a proof of randomness.

candidate_datasets.name: OEIS rule 30 center column
candidate_datasets.role: published center-column bits of elementary cellular automaton rule 30

candidate_datasets.name: OEIS binary expansion of pi
candidate_datasets.role: published binary digits of pi

candidate_datasets.name: NIST Random Bit Generation
candidate_datasets.role: public statistical test procedures for deviation from randomness

obstacles: Passing a finite battery of tests does not prove that no regularity exists.
The cellular-automaton analysis has to be limited to a stated class of simple rules.
rationale: Both sequences are published to great length, and block-frequency tests plus short cellular-automaton filters are standard computations. The claim asserts only that these analyses show no detectable deviation, which a significant failure would refute and a pass would support. It does not assert a proof that the sequences are random in every sense.

operationalization: Fix the sparsely sampled rule-30 keystream construction and compare the cost of the best published cryptanalysis with the published attack costs of standard stream ciphers. A cheaper complete break refutes 'at least as secure as any known system'; the absence of a break does not establish that equivalence.

candidate_datasets.name: NIST Computer Security Resource Center
candidate_datasets.role: public record of standardized ciphers and their evaluated security, as the comparison class

candidate_datasets.name: Golly
candidate_datasets.role: open generation of rule-30 output for the keystream construction under study

obstacles: 'Any known system' is an open-ended comparison class.
Sparse sampling changes the attack surface relative to earlier rule-30 proposals, so a break of one variant is not automatically a break of the other.
rationale: The cipher construction is explicit enough that published attack costs can be compared with those of standardized stream ciphers, using only public descriptions and generated keystream. That can refute a claim of matching the best known systems if a cheaper break exists for the stated variant. It cannot prove comparable security, because an undiscovered attack remains possible and the comparison class keeps growing.

operationalization: For substitution systems that generate nested patterns, search for a formula for each cell in a stated class of generalized hypergeometric functions. A uniform translation of every nested pattern into a fixed class would confirm the claim; escape into an ever-wider class of 'similar generalizations' leaves it unrefuted.

candidate_datasets.name: NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions
candidate_datasets.role: public definitions and identities for hypergeometric and generalized hypergeometric functions

obstacles: 'Suitably generalized' can be expanded until almost any nested formula counts.
Known closed forms for particular nested patterns do not yield a theorem for every substitution system.
rationale: Particular nested patterns, such as those tied to binomial coefficients modulo 2, have known formulas, and the hypergeometric class is a published, checkable target. The claim says any nested pattern, in functions that may be generalized as needed. Specific successes therefore test only a restricted scope, and the elastic generalization blocks a clean refutation.

operationalization: Compute minimal disjunctive-normal-form and Nand formula sizes for the state of rule 30 after t steps, and compare growth with rules 90 and 254. Rapid growth relative to those rules at accessible t supports the small-n evidence; a compact formula at large t, or slow growth, would refute 'no simple formula'.

candidate_datasets.name: Golly
candidate_datasets.role: open evolution of rule 30 and of the simple comparison rules 90 and 254

candidate_datasets.name: OEIS rule 30 center column
candidate_datasets.role: published rule-30 bits against which small formula sizes can be checked

obstacles: Exact minimal formulas become intractable as the light-cone width grows, so only small step counts are feasible.
Growth of one normal form does not rule out a compact formula in some other language.
rationale: Formula size after a few steps is a finite computation, and the contrast with rules 90 and 254 is well defined. Those small-n sizes can be recomputed and either continue the rapid growth Wolfram reports or break it. They do not prove that no simple formula exists for arbitrary step counts, nor the further claim about most cellular automata.

operationalization: Test whether successive neural populations, each depending on a fixed random subset of its inputs, produce codes that are stable under small input changes and that predict similarity-based retrieval. Such a layered random code matching behavior would support the mechanism; retrieval by similarity with a different circuit would leave the specific hashing claim unconfirmed.

candidate_datasets.name: CRCNS
candidate_datasets.role: public neural recordings during memory and sensory tasks

candidate_datasets.name: Human Connectome Project
candidate_datasets.role: public human brain-connectivity and behavioral data, at a coarser scale than layered hashing

obstacles: Similarity-based retrieval is compatible with several circuit designs.
Present recordings do not resolve whether each layer samples a fixed random set of inputs.
rationale: Behavioral and neural datasets can test whether memory retrieval is organized by similarity, which is the functional half of the claim. They do not resolve the proposed implementation, successive layers hashing random fixed input sets into codes stable under small changes. That mechanism remains one model among others consistent with the same public data.

operationalization: Across tasks that operationalize generalization, analogy, intuition, and deduction, test whether performance is predicted by similarity to stored instances rather than by application of content-free rules. A consistent memory-similarity account would support the claim; a dissociation in which logical performance tracks rule use and not retrieval would limit it.

candidate_datasets.name: OpenNeuro
candidate_datasets.role: public neuroimaging of reasoning and memory tasks, covering only some of the claimed cognitive domains

candidate_datasets.name: Human Connectome Project
candidate_datasets.role: public behavioral and imaging measures related to cognition, not a partition of thought into memory versus logic

obstacles: Almost any reasoning trace can be redescribed as retrieval of a learned pattern.
'Almost every major aspect of human thinking' has no fixed task list.
rationale: Cognitive datasets can address particular contrasts, such as analogy versus application of a stated rule. The claim says memory retrieval underlies almost all thinking and that logic itself is retrieved argument patterns. Those public resources cover fragments of that list, and most outcomes can be described in either the memory language or the rule language.

operationalization: Specify a small rule set claimed to be the core of thinking, show that its behavior is unchanged under changes of neural implementation, and compare it with human performance. A core that survives implementation changes and matches behavior would support the claim; essential dependence on particular neural detail would refute independence.

candidate_datasets.name: Human Connectome Project
candidate_datasets.role: public measurements of human brain structure and behavior, without an identified simple-rule core

candidate_datasets.name: Allen Brain Map
candidate_datasets.role: public neural-circuit detail of the kind the claim says the core does not depend on

obstacles: 'Rather simple rules' and 'a definite core' are not tied to a stated formal system.
Existing brain maps record neural detail; they do not contain a demonstration that thinking is independent of it.
rationale: The claim is that thinking has a core of simple rules largely independent of how neurons are built. Brain and behavior datasets record the neural detail and some performance, but they do not contain that core or a test of its implementation independence. Deciding the claim needs an explicit rule-level account that has not been produced.

operationalization: Compare the engineering cost and success of systems aimed at general human-like performance with systems aimed at declared specific tasks, and test whether human-like performance appears only after a human-like experience base. Systematically easier general systems would support the claim; systematically earlier and cheaper success on specific tasks would count against it.

candidate_datasets.name: GLUE benchmark
candidate_datasets.role: public task-specific language benchmarks, a proxy for restricted human-like tasks

candidate_datasets.name: MLCommons
candidate_datasets.role: public benchmark results comparing systems across defined tasks, not a measure of general human-like thought

obstacles: 'Easier' depends on how tasks are chosen and on research effort, which is not an experimental control.
General human-like thinking has no single public score comparable to task benchmarks.
rationale: Task-specific benchmarks and the public record of artificial systems give a partial, confounded comparison of narrow and broader aims. They do not measure 'general human-like thinking' on a scale that would cleanly show it is easier, and the further requirement of a human-like experience base is only loosely represented. The prediction is testable in part and not decided by current benchmarks.

operationalization: Identify 'recognizing all possible regularities' with deciding whether an arbitrary string has a short description, and apply the theorem that Kolmogorov complexity is uncomputable. A correct general decision procedure would refute the claim; the reduction to the halting problem confirms that no such procedure exists, while leaving particular methods free to catch particular regularities.

candidate_datasets.name: MathWorld: Kolmogorov Complexity
candidate_datasets.role: public statement that no algorithm computes description length in general

obstacles: The theorem bars a single method that works for every string; it does not limit what a given method finds in a given dataset, which the claim already allows.
rationale: The claim is that no method, however advanced, can in complete generality recognize every regularity and thus decide whether data have a simple description. That is the uncomputability of Kolmogorov complexity, which reduces to the halting problem and is a published proof. The claim's concession that stronger particular methods may catch more particular cases matches the theorem's scope rather than weakening the test.
